RV-01.title: Pilot network mechanism
RV-01.detail: Multicast video flooding an unmanaged switch that also carries networked audio. Rates and behavior are illustrative; the story keeps it 'supported, not proven' until the S01E01 tag.

RV-02.title: Hum fix that never lifts protective earth
RV-02.detail: Any hum or ground story must show the fix isolating the signal path and leaving every safety ground intact.

SB-01.title: Never defeat protective earth

RV-03.title: LED wall: moiré vs refresh banding
RV-03.detail: Two different effects that the prototype draws as one.

RV-05.title: Comb-filter worked example
RV-05.detail: Path lengths, delay and notch frequencies are illustrative geometry, not a measured room. Formula assumes two arrivals of similar level, no polarity inversion.

RV-14.title: Overhead work and exclusion zones
RV-14.detail: Overhead loudspeaker work is shown only by a qualified crew with a lift and a roped exclusion zone. Depiction must match current practice.

RV-17.title: Hearing exposure
RV-17.detail: Test signals and rehearsal levels are shown as moderate; earplugs offered. No level figures are given as guidance.

RV-18.title: Sanctuary kit topology
RV-18.detail: The booth, equipment room and overflow room layouts are invented; confirm they read as plausible.

RV-19.title: Color contrast
RV-19.detail: Chip, caption and bubble colors on panel washes need measured contrast in the final build.

RV-21.title: Representation: faith community, older adults, hearing-aid users
RV-21.detail: Worship, baptism, an 81-year-old hearing-aid user and characters of many backgrounds are depicted. Needs sensitivity reading and community consultation.

RV-24.title: Decision screens at phone width
RV-24.detail: The interactive choice cards need usability testing with target learners at 360 px.

RV-25.title: Gain staging, proximity effect and level-matched listening (new)
RV-25.detail: S01E02's mechanism: preamp gain set at speaking level clips at singing level; a directional mic gains low end up close; a louder version usually wins an unmatched comparison. All numbers (dB, trial counts, 'a hand's width') are illustrative.

RV-26.title: Electrical load arithmetic and circuit rules (new)
RV-26.detail: S01E05 shows a load estimate (P = V × I) with its assumptions stated. Wattages, voltages, breaker ratings and the 'don't run near the limit' planning rule are illustrative; the real rules are code- and site-specific and belong to a licensed electrician. Only the electrician opens the panel or resets the circuit.

RV-11.title: Accessibility findings and obligations
RV-11.detail: S01E06 shows an assistive listening system failing during speech. No legal requirement, standard or coverage figure is stated as fact; obligations vary by place and belong to an accessibility specialist and legal reviewer.

RV-04.title: DMX physical-layer teaching
RV-04.detail: DMX addressing, termination, splitting and cable guidance are simplified for teaching.

RV-15.title: Emergency and life-safety boundaries
RV-15.detail: S01E10 shows a power event. Life-safety systems (emergency lighting, alarms, exits) belong to the building and its responsible people; the story never has the AV team operate them.

RV-20.title: Level and evidence thresholds
RV-20.detail: Mission Control's level thresholds (L0–L3) and E-levels are provisional scoring rules.

RV-27.title: History breaks need a fact check
RV-27.detail: Every history break is a short summary written from general knowledge. Dates and attributions need a citation check before release.
RV-27.reviewer: Curriculum owner; historian or subject expert

RV-28.title: Fundamentals lessons and quizzes

RV-29.title: LED wall on camera: timing, standards and moiré (S01E07)
RV-29.detail: Refresh and scan banding, shutter timing, frame-rate families (50 / 59.94 / 60) and moiré are simplified for teaching. Processor menus, refresh figures and shutter values are illustrative; real walls and cameras differ by model.

RV-30.title: Budget, cost and risk figures (S01E08)

RV-31.title: Acceptance and commissioning practice (S01E09)
RV-31.detail: The acceptance workflow, test sheet, thresholds and sign-off are simplified from general commissioning practice. Not a standard or a contract form.

RV-32.title: Power loss, UPS runtimes and emergency lighting (S01E10)
RV-32.detail: The blackout, UPS runtimes and emergency-lighting behavior are illustrative. Emergency lighting, alarms and exits belong to the building and its responsible people; the AV team never restores, bypasses or tests them. Crowd guidance comes from the building's plan, not the booth.

RV-33.title: Video transport, codecs and streaming numbers
RV-33.detail: Bitrates, cable-length limits, latency and codec behavior in lessons and incidents are typical teaching values, not specifications.

RV-34.title: Board, budget and money conversations (S01E08)
RV-34.detail: A church owner board, a treasurer and a budget vote are depicted. Needs a reader familiar with volunteer-led organizations so the conflict is fair to every side.

RV-35.title: Wireless microphone spectrum rules
RV-35.detail: Which radio bands wireless microphones may use differs by country and changes over time. The lessons never name a band as legal; a frequency coordinator and current local rules decide.

RT-04.title: Broadcast practice is generic
RT-04.detail: Season 4 describes broadcast engineering (reference clocks, loudness targets, captions, STL links, bonded cellular, emergency relays) in generic terms with illustrative numbers. Real rules differ by country and regulator; a broadcast engineer and a regulatory reviewer should check every scene before release.

GT-01.title: Story gate and reviewer mode
GT-01.detail: The story is gated selectively at the owner's request: story decisions and one core hands-on skill per chapter must be finished before the pages after them open, and each chapter opens once the previous chapter's gates are cleared; every other interaction is optional. Reviewer mode (Mission Control) opens every page for authors and SMEs. Check that the gate never traps a reader (every lab has a way to finish; incidents always end) and that it suits screen-reader and keyboard users.

SR-01.title: Story ratings, Story Score and game over
SR-01.detail: Six ratings (Competence, Evidence discipline, Trust, Safety/authority, Technical debt, Leadership/readiness) are computed from first attempts: decisions (tagged by what they test), quizzes, drills, labs, live incidents, meltdowns and skipped checks. The Story Score is their weighted mean (22/18/15/20/12/13%). Every season finale ends with a review; below 65 the story ends and the reader retries the season or restarts. The Season 9 review locks a Seasons 10–12 loadout (budget, team, monitoring, redundancy, authority, documentation); weak ratings leave the bare minimum, and S10–12 options can require loadout levels. Weights and thresholds are design choices to tune with playtesting.

RV-176.title: Who owns what in a recording studio (Season 10)
RV-176.detail: The artist owns her performance and decides every use of it beyond what her contract already allows — stems, clips, copies, anything that leaves the building; the label owns the release, its schedule and its delivery specification under its contract with her; the studio's owner (Hollis) owns the studio, its rooms, its policies and its purchases; a licensed electrician owns the circuits and the earthing; a qualified technician repairs mains-powered instruments; the mastering engineer and the artist own the sound of the master. She never copies or sends a performance without the artist's written OK, never defeats a protective earth and never overrules the artist's own call about her voice.

RV-187.title: Who owns what in a global estate (Season 12)
RV-187.detail: The CIO owns the room standard, the change board and every acceptance of risk; each regional head owns their region's approved variants; each site's facilities team owns its power, cooling and anything overhead; the network owner owns the WAN and its quality of service; security owns named accounts, the vault and remote access; procurement owns vendor selection and contracts; each technician owns the rooms they support and may refuse an unsafe or unapproved change. Maya owns the architecture, the drafts, the training and the evidence. She never makes herself the only admin, the only contact or the only person who understands a decision.

RV-188.title: Season 12 figures are illustrative
RV-188.detail: Room counts, ages, costs, reserves, depreciation, failure rates, rollout stages, detection and restore times, flicker frequencies, vendor scores and budgets are invented or simplified for teaching. Real estates follow their owners' finance, engineering and procurement rules.

RV-189.title: Juniors, refusals and blame (Season 12)
RV-189.detail: Juniors are shown as capable professionals who can stop unsafe or unapproved work and are backed for it in writing. Reviews are blameless; nobody is shamed for an honest mistake or for asking. Nothing in the story is HR or employment advice.

RV-190.title: Accessibility in the standard (Season 12)
RV-190.detail: Captions, assistive listening and accessible controls are shown as requirements of the standard, not extras. The story is not legal advice on accessibility law; real obligations vary by country and are confirmed with the organisation's accessibility lead and counsel.

RV-191.title: Invented firm, sites, vendors and products (Season 12)
RV-191.detail: Fenwright Group, its offices, regions, vendors, platforms and products, and every person in Season 12 are invented and must not resemble a real organisation or product.

FX-01.title: Formula cards need a technical check
FX-01.detail: Every math and physics problem shows a formula card (name, equation, symbol legend) and a worked equation. The cards use textbook forms with simplified assumptions (free field, 343 m/s at about 20 °C, planning-level power figures). A subject-matter expert should check each card before release.
FX-01.reviewer: Audio / video / RF / network SMEs; curriculum owner

TL-01.title: Skill ladder (Beginner → Mastery)
TL-01.detail: Three seasons per support level: Seasons 1–3 Beginner (term, definition, formula, variables, worked example), 4–6 Intermediate (formula and variables), 7–9 Advanced (formula on request) and 10–12 Mastery (reference only; the learner chooses the tool and says why). Beginner means more support, not lower stakes. Teaching scenes and notebook cards were added to every chapter; S1–S3 also carry the Empathia Learn Fieldbook modules (FB-01). Worked examples are illustrative. Readers can change the support level on Mission Control.

RV-37.title: Fix-It Lab simulators are simplified models
RV-37.detail: Signal levels add as powers, EQ uses a textbook peaking filter, comb filtering assumes two arrivals, camera blur/moiré/banding use toy models, and network reachability ignores routing. Thresholds and every figure are illustrative and need a subject-matter review.
RV-37.reviewer: Audio, video, lighting and network SMEs

RV-38.title: Labs never replace qualified people
RV-38.detail: Power and rigging labs are planning worksheets for the qualified person (electrician, rigger). Nothing in a lab is an instruction to open a panel, move a load or change someone else's network.

RV-39.title: Physics simulations are toy models
RV-39.detail: The Physics in Motion simulations (interference, inverse square, diffraction, speed of sound, loop gain, Ohm's law, sampling, path loss, color mixing, Fourier series, Sabine, quantization, thin lens, beam reactions, password entropy) use textbook formulas with simplified geometry and illustrative numbers. Science-history notes need a citation check.

UX-01.title: UX rules are simplified design principles
UX-01.detail: Each episode's UX rule paraphrases a well-known usability principle (visibility of status, recognition over recall, error prevention, Fitts's law and others) in story terms. Needs a UX/accessibility review.

WT-01.title: Decision weight and crew trust are story devices
WT-01.detail: Merit and crew-trust changes after each choice are simple heuristics that make consequences visible. They are not a judgment of real people or a competency score.

RP-01.title: Role-playing layer needs an author pass
RP-01.detail: Quest cards, dialogue beats, dialogue choices and discoveries were added across Seasons 1–4 at the owner's request (game-style storytelling: humor, awkward moments, darker and mysterious turns). They sit between the existing panels and do not change them. The author should read each episode end to end for voice, continuity and tone.

MD-01.title: Meltdown simulations are illustrative
MD-01.detail: Meltdown boss fights model cascading failure with a toy dependency engine and invented timings (grace periods, dark-time budgets, story-clock rate). They teach order of operations — contain, fail over, verify, and stay inside boundaries — not real system behaviour.

MD-02.title: Boundaries inside meltdowns
MD-02.detail: Every meltdown includes actions that cross a safety or authority line (touching power gear, sending people onto towers or flood roads, staying against an evacuation order, airing unverified safety claims). Choosing one ends the mission immediately. Reviewers should confirm each boundary text matches the owner in the series rules.

GL-01.title: Glossary definitions are teaching definitions
GL-01.detail: Glossary entries are simplified, plain-language definitions written for learners, not standards or legal definitions. Several are SIGNAL conventions (e.g. the evidence states). A subject-matter reviewer should confirm each domain's entries.

PR-01.title: Prologue redrawn from the prototype
PR-01.detail: The prototype's eleven chapters are the novel's opening Prologue. Dialogue, narration and field notes are the owner's words unchanged (brand name updated to Empathia Learn); the drawings are redrawn in the novel's style so speech never covers a diagram. The original file is archived unchanged at the back. An illustrator pass is still pending (VR-01).

FB-01.title: Fieldbook curriculum (Seasons 1–3)
FB-01.detail: Seasons 1–3 teach the owner's Technical Fieldbook (renamed the Empathia Learn Fieldbook), one module per chapter, at Beginner support. Starting points (compressor settings, EQ ranges, level targets, lux ranges) are the Fieldbook's rules of thumb, labelled illustrative. Brand and product names in the source were replaced with generic descriptions.

FB-02.title: Fieldbook formula corrections
FB-02.detail: Corrected while adapting the Fieldbook: (1) a power ratio in decibels is 10·log₁₀(P₂/P₁); 20·log₁₀ applies to voltage or pressure. (2) P = 10^((L−30)/10) converts dBm (not dBu) to watts. (3) The stream loudness range '−12 to −6 LUFS' is louder than the typical platform normalization target (about −14 LUFS integrated, platform-dependent); lessons use −14 and say to check the platform. (4) Perceived brightness of a large screen does not follow the inverse-square law the way a small fixture's illuminance does. (5) Sound covers 1,000 ft in about 0.89 s. (6) The upward-center-fill example was recomputed (6 m extra path → about 17.5 ms → first notch near 29 Hz).

FB-03.title: Fieldbook safety adaptations
FB-03.detail: Where a Fieldbook story involves climbing, panels or overhead work, the novel keeps the lesson but not the act: nobody climbs during a live event, electricians own panels and breakers, riggers and structural engineers own anything overhead. Protective earth is never lifted to cure hum.

CH-01.title: Challenge modes are teaching models
CH-01.detail: HEAR IT · SEE IT · REACH IT · BUILD IT · RECORD IT use standard physics — a log-domain feed-forward compressor (Giannoulis, Massberg & Reiss 2012), RBJ biquads, Karplus–Strong synthesis, thin-lens depth of field, exposure value, sinusoidal flicker integration, a defocus-disk MTF with an OLPF and Bayer sampling for moiré, WCAG 2 contrast and the Machado (2009) colour-vision simulation, uniform-cone photometry, Sabine/Eyring reverberation, bits-per-pixel and upload headroom, two- and three-transmitter intermodulation, mic sensitivity/EIN gain structure, the 3-to-1 rule and BS.1770 gated loudness. Targets are teaching windows: a professional may choose differently on purpose. Gear is generic; no product is modelled; the humorous wrong answers are jokes with a real explanation.
CH-01.reviewer: Audio engineer; video engineer; lighting designer; acoustician; RF coordinator

BOSS-01.title: Boss-level alarm light and photosensitivity
BOSS-01.detail: The boss level tints the edge of the screen yellow, red or green as the owner asked. It pulses at most once per second with soft ramps and limited area, well inside the three-flashes-per-second guidance (WCAG 2.3.1); with reduced motion or ‘calm lights’ it is a steady tint. Strobe looks in the cue challenge are shown as a gentle 2 Hz pulse at low contrast. Review with an accessibility specialist before public release.

BOSS-02.title: Commission figures are illustrative (Episode 11, Seasons 8–12)
BOSS-02.detail: Unit prices, labour hours and rates, tax and contingency percentages, running costs, equipment power, weight, heat, PoE, bandwidth, latency, storage and support-hour figures in the boss commissions are invented for teaching. Real estimates come from quotations, site surveys and the engineers of record; power belongs to the electrician, loads overhead to the structural engineer and rigger, cooling to the mechanical engineer, the network to its owner, access to security.
BOSS-02.reviewer: Cost estimator; AV systems designer; electrical and mechanical engineers of record

RV-40.title: Touring RF coordination (S02E01–E02)
RV-40.detail: Sixteen-channel plans, per-city scans, spare frequencies, 'local services' and every frequency, level and margin figure are illustrative. No band is named as legal; which frequencies a touring show may use depends on the country, the city and current rules.

RV-41.title: Overhead work is shown only as plans, drawings and conversation (S02E01–E04)
RV-41.detail: Rigging points, beam ratings, ground-supported truss and load budgets are depicted only as people discussing documents and a video call. Nobody is shown under a load, climbing, or performing a rigging procedure, and no figure is guidance. Stop-work is shown as normal.

RV-42.title: Antennas, line of sight and body absorption (S02E02 · CASE-007)
RV-42.detail: The drop-out mechanism (antennas moved behind a steel LED frame, a performer's back turned, signal falling into the noise) is the SIGNAL adaptation. Signal levels, noise floors, dB losses and meter readings are illustrative.

RV-43.title: Temporary power interface (S02E01 · lesson P2)
RV-43.detail: Generators, distribution boxes and tie-ins are described only as who-does-what. The tie-in, any panel, generator earthing and anything wet belong to a qualified electrician or the power vendor. Nothing here is a connection procedure.

RV-44.title: Console update, fixture profiles and default fade times (S02E04 · CASE-012)
RV-44.detail: MS-08's mechanism in SIGNAL form: an update replaced one fixture type's profile and reset the show's default fade time. Pan/tilt ranges, fade times, file timestamps and the rollback arithmetic are illustrative; real consoles differ.

RV-45.title: Stage management authority; fly and scenery cues (S02E04)
RV-45.detail: The stage manager holds and stops the show; fly and scenery cues run only as rehearsed, on the stage manager's call. The booth never improvises a fly move and never stops a show on its own.
RV-45.reviewer: Professional stage manager; theatre safety reviewer

RV-46.title: In-ear templates, mix-minus and delayed returns (S02E01, S02E05)
RV-46.detail: The IFB/in-ear routing, return delays (about a third of a second), and the delayed-auditory-feedback effect are simplified and illustrative. No level or delay figure is a specification.

RV-47.title: Public blame, apology and workplace conflict (S02E03, S02E05)
RV-47.detail: A lighting director calls a rigger a coward in front of a crew; a festival organizer blames a monitor engineer online; Maya admits a mistake in public. Needs a reader who has worked touring crews so every side is fair and nobody reads as a villain.

RV-48.title: Show networks on the road (lesson N2, S02E04)
RV-48.detail: Cable-run limits, redundancy and switch behavior are typical teaching values. Real designs depend on the equipment and the venue.

RV-49.title: Screens, documents and drawings inside panels are generic
RV-49.detail: Advance packets, venue drawings, video calls, console screens, phone clips and plots are invented and schematic. None may resemble a real product interface, a real venue's drawing or a usable rigging document.

RV-50.title: Room combining, partition sensors and control states (S02E06 · lesson C1)
RV-50.detail: The house room-combine model (a partition sensor on the airwall track, an interlock, a COMBINED state that plays one room's inputs everywhere and ignores the other room's plates) is the SIGNAL adaptation. Real systems differ by design and programmer; the hotel's system, its sensor and any override belong to the hotel's AV team.
RV-50.reviewer: AV control programmer; hotel AV manager

RV-51.title: Hotel banquet and housekeeping staff (S02E06)
RV-51.detail: The comedy cold open involves a banquet captain, a houseperson and a vacuum. The joke must land on the situation, never on hospitality workers: the wall crew did their job correctly, and the story says so.

RV-52.title: Stream tap points, stems and A/V sync (S02E07 · CASE-008 · lesson V8)
RV-52.detail: Whether a pre-fader send also ignores the channel mute and processing differs by console and by setting; the 'input tap' template, the post-fader mistake, the frame latency of the video path and the 40 ms audio delay are illustrative. The case mechanism is SIGNAL's adaptation of the Fieldbook's livestream-recording case (p. 154) — owner to confirm (Q-004).

RV-53.title: Show control, cue lists, change freezes and pre-show checklists (S02E08 · lesson L8)
RV-53.detail: The four-cue opening, the freeze time, the split checklist hour and every checklist line are illustrative production practice, not a standard. Real productions set their own freeze and change rules; the stage manager calls the show.
RV-53.reviewer: Production manager; stage manager; show-control specialist

RV-54.title: SDI one-cable failure, floor pockets and cable paths (S02E08 · CASE-009)
RV-54.detail: The crushed connector, cable reach figures and the rerouted spare are illustrative (see RV-33). Floor pockets can also hold power outlets: the power side belongs to the venue's electrician and is never opened by the AV crew. Cable across a guest path is shown only as a refused option.
RV-54.reviewer: Video engineer; venue electrician; event safety reviewer

RV-55.title: Addressing, DHCP and the 1 a.m. workaround (S02E09 · lesson N3)
RV-55.detail: Address ranges, pool sizes, gateway numbers, lease behavior (pools filling 'from the bottom') and the conflict symptoms are illustrative; real DHCP servers differ, and some check for conflicts. The workaround is deliberately flawed (DEBT-003) and must never read as a recommended design. The site network belongs to the site team.

RV-56.title: Weather holds, lightning and flash-to-bang (S02E10)
RV-56.detail: Authority to hold or stop an outdoor show belongs to the production's written weather plan and the person it names (Ben, with production and the stage manager) — never FOH. Flash-to-bang distances, the hold trigger, the 30-minute all-clear and every time on the page are illustrative, never guidance. Nobody works on a structure, overhead, or at wet power during weather; shelter follows the event's own safety plan.
RV-56.reviewer: Event safety officer; meteorologist; production manager

RV-57.title: Sensitivity: the 2011 stage-collapse history break (S02E10)
RV-57.detail: The history break describes a real event in which people died and many were injured. No imagery; plain, respectful wording; no blame beyond the published findings; dates, numbers and findings need a citation check (see RV-27). Consider whether to consult people connected to the event before release.

RV-58.title: Generators, distribution and wet outdoor power (S02E10)
RV-58.detail: Generators, distros and anything electrical near water belong to the power vendor's qualified technician (Hank) or an electrician. The alarm, its cause and the sign-off are illustrative and shown only as who-does-what, never as a procedure. Re-seating an energized connector in water is shown only as a refused, incident-ending choice.

RV-59.title: In-ear monitoring, talkback and the local fallback mixer (S02E10 · lesson A10)
RV-59.detail: The in-ear, talkback and fallback-mixer arrangement is illustrative. No listening levels are given; hearing health belongs to the performer and their audiologist (see RV-17). Wireless-channel counts, antenna readings and the crushed-cable loss are illustrative (see RV-35).
RV-59.reviewer: Monitor engineer; RF coordinator; hearing specialist

RV-60.title: Identity and room accounts (S03E01)
RV-60.detail: Room accounts, password-expiry policy, sign-in sessions, restarts and a 'room-account policy' with managed credentials are simplified and deliberately generic. Real identity systems differ in how sessions, expiry and device sign-in behave; no product or platform behavior is described.

RV-65.title: Workplace pressure, burnout and blame (Season 3)
RV-65.detail: Season 3 depicts a VP's pressure on support staff, an engineer's quiet burnout, a new manager who feels mocked by IT, and a reorganization announcement about people's jobs. Needs a sensitivity read so no role reads as a villain and distress is portrayed with care.

RV-66.title: Enterprise figures are illustrative (Season 3)
RV-66.detail: Room counts (about 300; 289 in the inventory), ring sizes, attendee numbers, ticket counts, percentages and deal sizes are invented for the story. None is a benchmark.

RV-67.title: Generic workplace screens (Season 3)
RV-67.detail: Touch panels, change records, dashboards, ticket queues, sign-in errors and call screens are invented. They must not resemble a real conferencing, identity, ticketing or operating-system interface, wording or logo.

RV-68.title: Access and authority boundaries in the workplace
RV-68.detail: Security owns access decisions; the identity team owns accounts; the network owner owns ports and segments. The story never shows AV staff resetting, sharing or exempting credentials, or re-patching the network, as a working fix. Decisions that cross these lines are marked as failures.

RV-69.title: Early password history anecdotes (S03E01)
RV-69.detail: The 1960s time-sharing password stories (first passwords; a password file shown to every user) are retold from secondary accounts by people who worked there. Dates and details need a citation check.

RV-61.title: Acoustic echo cancellation, applied twice (S03E02)
RV-61.detail: Echo cancellers, references, re-adaptation, double-talk and the effect of two cancellers in series are simplified for teaching. Real behavior depends on the processor, the software and the room. Delays, levels and echo-reduction figures are illustrative.

RV-62.title: USB enumeration, power states and extenders (S03E03)
RV-62.detail: Selective suspend, re-enumeration as a new device instance, extender behavior, port power budgets and USB cable-length figures are simplified teaching values. Real behavior depends on the computer, the operating system's power policy, the extender and the software; no product is described.

RV-63.title: Network segments and VLANs for AV (S03E04)
RV-63.detail: VLAN assignment, multicast audio staying inside its segment, control traffic crossing a firewall, addresses (10.80 / 10.40) and port names are simplified and invented. Real designs differ; the network owner decides and changes port assignments.

RV-64.title: Monitoring, telemetry and inventory (S03E05)
RV-64.detail: Polling by ping, last-known-state caching, staleness thresholds, inventory-driven dashboards and the 'meeting started clean within two minutes' outcome metric are simplified illustrations of monitoring practice. Percentages and counts are invented.

RV-70.title: Room control as a state machine; scheduling race (S03E06)
RV-70.detail: The Cedar Room's states, events, macros, the end-of-booking sweep, display warm-up behavior, codec standby refusal and calendar-push timing are invented and simplified for teaching. Real control platforms differ; timings are illustrative.

RV-76.title: Workplace burnout and a colleague thinking of quitting (Sam, S03E06–E08)
RV-76.detail: Sam's exhaustion, self-criticism and a drafted resignation are shown with care and without a quick fix. Needs a reader with workplace-wellbeing experience so it neither trivializes burnout nor turns it into a lesson prop.

RV-78.title: Illustrative fleet figures and timings (S03E06–E10)
RV-78.detail: Room counts, ticket counts, timings, costs, test-ring sizes and every clock value in Season 3's second half are invented for the story. None is a benchmark.

RV-71.title: Usability testing and meeting-room accessibility (S03E07)
RV-71.detail: Test method (five participants, think-aloud, no helping), reach zones, panel heights, feedback timing and listening-system feeds are simplified and illustrative. No legal requirement, standard clause or dimension is stated as fact; obligations vary by place and belong to an accessibility specialist and legal reviewer.
RV-71.reviewer: Accessibility specialist; UX researcher; legal reviewer

RV-72.title: Representation in S03E07–E10: disabled colleagues; Ray and Mei in conflict
RV-72.detail: S03E07's wheelchair user and hearing-aid user are colleagues with expertise and humor, not problems to be solved; the seated figure and hearing-aid drawing are placeholder art. S03E09–E10's Ray and Mei disagree for good reasons: neither is a villain, Mei is never framed as cold, Ray never as careless or malicious. Needs disabled readers and a sensitivity read.
RV-72.reviewer: Disabled readers; disability-community consultation; sensitivity reader; security professional

RV-73.title: Speech intelligibility and microphone coverage (A12, S03E07)
RV-73.detail: Coverage zones, the inverse-square estimate, speech-to-noise examples and listening-system feeds are simplified teaching values, not design targets.

RV-79.title: DEBT-003 inside the room standard (S03E07, S03E10)
RV-79.detail: Section 5.3 copies the Riverbend workaround: fixed addresses at the top of each automatic range, not excluded from automatic assignment. It is depicted as a flaw on purpose (dramatic irony). The network owner should confirm the failure it predicts (duplicate addresses as the automatic pool fills) is described accurately and non-instructionally.

RV-74.title: Incident, problem and change practice (S03E08, M2, CASE-016)
RV-74.detail: Service-management terms (incident, problem, known error, standard/normal/emergency change, change board) follow common practice but are simplified and not tied to any published framework's wording. Legacy-scheduler behavior, addresses and timings are invented.

RV-75.title: Security content is generic and non-instructional (S03E09, S2)
RV-75.detail: Remote-access models, accounts, second factors, gateways and recordings are described only as ideas. No real tool, platform, operating system or vendor is named or depicted, and nothing is a procedure. Security owns access decisions; the story shows crossing that line as a failure.

RV-77.title: Room computer content capture, update rings and exception registers (S03E10, MS-02, M3, CASE-015)
RV-77.detail: The overnight update, the 'first input detected' default, the two-input ingest box, ring sizes, the fleet query and the fallback card are invented and simplified. Real conferencing platforms and endpoint-management tools differ; no product behavior is claimed.

RV-86.title: Timing references simplified (S04E01)
RV-86.detail: Satellite-disciplined reference clocks, holdover, black burst, a gateway's lock range and a 20 ppm holdover drift are simplified and illustrative. Real plants use specific timing standards and redundancy designs; a broadcast engineer should check every line.

RV-87.title: A/V sync figures simplified (S04E02)
RV-87.detail: The 167 ms stream video latency, the acceptability window (sound no more than ~15 ms early, ~45 ms late) and the flash-and-beep method are simplified planning figures. Real tolerances come from broadcast recommendations and differ by service.

RV-88.title: Loudness targets and meters simplified (S04E03)
RV-88.detail: The −24 LUFS target, ±2 LU tolerance, segment readings and the 'perceived loudness doubles per 10 LU' rule of thumb are illustrative. Real targets differ by country, regulator and service.

RV-89.title: Caption transport simplified (S04E04)
RV-89.detail: Caption data riding in a video signal's ancillary space, a transcoder profile that discards it, caption-present monitoring and data-rate figures are simplified. Real caption standards and regulations differ by country; a broadcast engineer and a captioning professional should review.

RV-90.title: Microwave link figures simplified (S04E05)
RV-90.detail: Rain fade (γ = k·R^α), fade margins, Fresnel clearance, the 18 km hop, 7 GHz and the other-carrier IP fallback are simplified and illustrative. Real link design uses regional rain statistics and licensed engineers.

RV-91.title: Tower and transmitter boundaries (S04E05)
RV-91.detail: Only the licensed transmitter engineer operates the transmitter. Tower work is by a certified tower crew only, never in wind, ice or lightning, and never depicted as a procedure. No character climbs or stands near the tower in the storm.

RV-92.title: Bonded cellular and capacity simplified (S04E06)
RV-92.detail: Bonded modems, a fixed 12 Mb/s preset, adaptive floors, 5 MHz per link, the crowd SNR and a 50% usable share are illustrative. Real kits and networks behave differently.

RV-93.title: Invented school sports event (S04E06)
RV-93.detail: The state semifinal, schools and stadium are invented; no real league, team or venue.

RV-94.title: Addressing and DHCP simplified (S04E07)
RV-94.detail: The /24, the automatic range .10–.250, the reserved block and the conflict behaviour are simplified and invented. Real address management differs; the network owner decides.

RV-95.title: Security incident kept generic (S04E08)
RV-95.detail: The phishing email, account lockout, resets and segmentation are described without techniques. Security (Quinn) owns every access decision; the story never shows AV staff unlocking, resetting or sharing credentials. A security professional should review.

RV-96.title: Failover drill and timecode simplified (S04E09)
RV-96.detail: The backup MCR, its reference and timecode generator, the two-frame overnight drift, rollback criteria and caption setup are simplified and illustrative. Real failover plans are specific to each plant.

RV-97.title: Emergency information boundaries (S04E10)
RV-97.detail: Forecasts and alerts belong to the agencies that issue them and are relayed word for word; evacuation orders belong to the county emergency manager; field pull-backs belong to the news director's field safety plan; the generator and transfer switch belong to the power vendor and the facilities electrician. Unverified reports are routed to officials, never aired. Nobody enters flood water on the page.

RV-98.title: Flood timeline and figures illustrative (S04E10)
RV-98.detail: River levels, the 1964 line, crest times, travel speeds, audience counts and shelter numbers are invented for the story.

RV-125.title: Patient privacy in the story (S05E02)
RV-125.detail: Maya never views, joins or records a real consult and never enters a room during one. Testing uses the simulation lab's training manikin and a staff test account. Any recording or monitoring of clinical calls is decided by the hospital's privacy officer. Clinical workflows are simplified.

RV-126.title: Hearing-loop figures simplified (S05E03)
RV-126.detail: Field strengths (mA/m), the 400 mA/m reference, the 12 dB metal loss and the supplementary loop are simplified and illustrative. Real loops are designed and commissioned to published standards by qualified installers, with a documented field-strength survey.

RV-127.title: PoE figures simplified (S05E04)
RV-127.detail: Switch budgets, per-camera draw by day and night, shedding order and port priority are simplified and illustrative. Real PoE budgets, classes and priority behavior depend on the equipment and are set by the network owner.

RV-128.title: Exam integrity and security cameras (S05E04)
RV-128.detail: Whether exam-room cameras record, and in what mode, is campus security's and the exams office's decision, under the university's privacy policy. AV never turns off, re-aims or re-schedules a security camera; the story shows Maya asking Delgado, who decides.

RV-129.title: Echo cancellation simplified (S05E05)
RV-129.detail: Acoustic echo cancellation, its reference signal, delays and the preset/snapshot system are simplified and illustrative; real DSP platforms differ. One-way and round-trip delays are story figures.

RV-130.title: Auto-mixer and coverage simplified (S05E06)
RV-130.detail: Ceiling-array lobes, gating thresholds, speech levels and the recording level check are simplified and illustrative; real arrays and auto-mixers behave differently by design.

RV-131.title: Measuring recordings without listening (S05E06)
RV-131.detail: The new outcome check measures speech level in lecture recordings, with no one listening to content. What is measured, and who may see it, is agreed with the teaching office and faculty under the university's recording policy. Grant consents to Maya hearing his own recordings.

RV-132.title: Emergency alerts belong to the emergency manager (S05E07)
RV-132.detail: Only the campus emergency manager writes, approves and sends alerts; tests happen in her scheduled windows using her verbatim TEST template. AV and IT carry the message and measure the path — they never compose, edit, delay or add to it. Hold times and channel rules are the emergency manager's decisions.

RV-133.title: Alert-path timings illustrative (S05E07)
RV-133.detail: Stage latencies, the polling interval, the hub's hold and the push gateway are simplified and invented for the story; they are not requirements or product behavior.

RV-134.title: Clock drift and time sources simplified (S05E08)
RV-134.detail: The hub's 50 ppm holdover drift, the offsets, the slewing behavior and the three-source vote are simplified and illustrative. Real time distribution uses specified protocols, oscillators and monitoring chosen by the network owner.

RV-135.title: Lifecycle figures illustrative (S05E09)
RV-135.detail: Failure counts, rates, warranty terms, prices and the budget are invented for the story; they are not product reliability data or a real vendor's terms.

RV-136.title: Commencement stream figures illustrative (S05E10)
RV-136.detail: Bit rates, uplink capacity, viewer counts, the station's take and the direct contribution path are simplified and invented; they are not product settings or broadcast requirements.

RV-137.title: Interpreters and captioners as professionals (S05E10)
RV-137.detail: The interpreter and the captioner are shown as skilled professionals with the right to the feeds they need; the story needs review by working interpreters and captioners.

RV-145.title: Structure and projection mounts (Season 6)
RV-145.detail: Where a projector hangs, what carries it and whether a beam can be penetrated are decided by the structural engineer and the architect. The story shows the AV designer proposing a lens and a position with numbers, never designing a mount or altering structure.

RV-146.title: Clinical systems in record drawings (Season 6)
RV-146.detail: Nurse call and every clinical system are owned by the hospital's clinical engineering team; the story shows AV staff marking and avoiding clinical ports, never patching, testing or re-labelling them. Patient-safety details are illustrative.

RV-147.title: Multicast, IGMP snooping and queriers (Season 6)
RV-147.detail: What a switch does with multicast when snooping is on but no querier is present differs by make and firmware (some flood, some prune after membership times out). Stream rates, port speeds and lighting protocol rates are illustrative; real designs follow the audio and lighting manufacturers' network guides and the venue IT team's standards.

RV-156.title: UPS runtime and heartbeat figures (Season 7)
RV-156.detail: Runtime = battery energy × efficiency ÷ load is a first estimate; real runtime falls faster at high loads and with battery age, and facilities use the maker's runtime chart and live readings. Heartbeat intervals and timeouts differ by product and network; the figures are illustrative.
